One declared link from an owner component to the components that may fill it.

kind and key name the acceptable targets: kind names one or several component kinds, key (when non-empty) narrows to specific keys within those kinds, matched through ComponentIdentity.satisfies. many marks a relation that binds several components at once; optional marks one that may stay unbound or be left empty, and says nothing else: on_delete alone decides what deleting a bound target does, block refusing the deletion while this relation holds the target and detach letting it through and dropping the binding. default and has_fallback together describe a relation that can be resolved without an explicit binding.

items.title: lookback
items.text:
lookback(now: date, lookback: int, offset: int = 1, granularity: TimeGranularity = <TimeGranularity.DAY: 'day'>, start: date | None = None) -> TimePartitionWindow | None

Build the trailing window a scheduled workload should cover.

The window is counted in partitions, never in days: offset is how many partitions back from the current one the window ends, and lookback is how many it spans. At daily granularity, offset=1, lookback=1 is "yesterday only" and offset=0 includes the current (still incomplete) partition.

The caller's timezone reaches the window through now: passing an aware datetime localized to a zone makes DAY, MONTH and YEAR windows follow that zone's calendar. HOUR windows are the deliberate exception: an aware now is normalized back to UTC (see coerce_to_datetime), because hour partition keys are naive-UTC labels and zones on a fractional offset do not align to UTC hour boundaries at all.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default now date

The reference instant, in whatever timezone the caller labels partitions with.

required lookback int

How many partitions the window spans (at least 1).

required offset int

How many partitions back from the current one the window ends.

1 granularity TimeGranularity

The period one partition covers.

<TimeGranularity.DAY: 'day'> start date | None

Optional lower bound (an asset's earliest partition) to clamp the window to.

None

Returns:

Type Description TimePartitionWindow | None

The window, or None if clamping to start leaves it empty.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If lookback is below 1, or offset is negative.

The decorated class's annotations and attributes become the Config subclass body. Since Config extends BaseSettings, fields can still be loaded from environment variables.

relations maps a relation name to a Relation, a component class, or a list of component classes narrowing the relation the decorated class declares under that name. Every other keyword is one of the public ClassVars and field defaults the decorated class declares, or Config itself for a plain class (key, name, icon, tags). An unknown name is a TypeError at decoration.

items.title: FetchField
items.text:
FetchField(
    default: Any = Ellipsis,
    *,
    provider: str,
    label_key: str = "name",
    value_key: str = "id",
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> Any

Field whose options are fetched from a resource's provider method.

The backend instantiates the resource bound to the relation <name> (from the credentials the form already holds) and calls the fetch_field_provider method <method> on it. The lookup logic lives next to the credentials it uses; there is no per-provider API route to hand-write.

The dependency is the provider's own relation (the <name> part): the frontend waits for that resource to be selected, then resolves via /components/resolve. It is implicit in provider, so there is no separate depends_on.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default default Any

Default value (... means required).

Ellipsis provider str

"<name>.<method>" reference to a @fetch_field_provider method on the resource bound to the relation <name>.

required label_key str

Key in each response item used as the display label.

'name' value_key str

Key in each response item used as the stored value.

'id' **kwargs Any

Forwarded to pydantic.Field. Pass discriminator=True to mark the field as the component's instance discriminator.

required

Returns:

Type Description Any

A Pydantic Field descriptor.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If provider is not of the form "<name>.<method>".

Example: 

account_id: str = FetchField(
    provider="connection.accounts",
    label_key="name",
    value_key="account_id",
)

items.title: fetch_field_provider
items.text:
fetch_field_provider(fn: F) -> F

Mark a resource method as a FetchField data source.

A FetchField(provider="<name>.<method>") resolves its options by instantiating the resource bound to the relation <name> (from the credentials the form already holds) and calling the method named <method>. Only methods marked with this decorator may be invoked that way; it is the allowlist that stops the browser from calling arbitrary attributes.

The method runs inside the API process, which installs the connection classes but not their heavy provider SDK extras, so a provider must use lightweight HTTP (httpx2), never self.api (the SDK client).

It returns a list[dict]; the FetchField picks label_key / value_key out of each item:

class FacebookAdsConnection(il.Connection):
    @il.fetch_field_provider
    async def accounts(self) -> list[dict]:
        ...

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default fn F

The resource method to mark as an options provider.

required

Type Description F

The same callable, stamped as a fetch provider.

items.title: Schemas & normalization
items.text: A schema is an asset's data contract; a normalizer coerces the vendor's rows into it and a materialization strategy decides how they land.

items.title: schema
items.text:
schema(target: Any = None, /, **settings: Any) -> Any

Create a Schema subclass from a decorated class.

Can be used bare or with arguments:

@schema
class UserSchema:
    id: int
    name: str
    email: str

@schema(key="custom", name="Custom Schema")
class OtherSchema:
    value: float

The decorated class's annotations and attributes become the Schema subclass body. key overrides the auto-derived snake_cased key and name is the human-readable display name.

items.title: Schema
items.text:
Schema(**data: Any)

Bases: interloper.serializable.base.Serializable

Defines the expected output structure of an asset.

Subclass to declare output fields:

class UserSchema(Schema):
    id: int
    name: str
    email: str

Class methods provide schema operations on list[dict] data:

Schema.infer(rows)
UserSchema.validate_rows(rows)
UserSchema.reconcile(rows)

Examines the values across all rows for each key and maps Python types to Pydantic field types. All fields are Optional because any key may be absent in some rows.

items.title: reconcile
items.text:
reconcile(
    rows: list[dict[str, Any]],
) -> list[dict[str, Any]]

Reconcile rows against this schema.

Fields are coerced one by one through per-field TypeAdapters — the row-wise mirror of the DataFrame representation's column-wise casts. Extra keys are dropped (their union logged as a warning), missing fields get their default (or None, which pydantic accepts only for nullable fields), and scalar str fields are stringified up front since pydantic's lax mode never coerces to str.

This is more permissive than validate_rows: it actively transforms data to match the schema rather than rejecting mismatches.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default rows list[dict[str, Any]]

List of row dicts.

required

Returns:

Type Description list[dict[str, Any]]

A new list of row dicts with columns aligned and types coerced.

Raises:

Type Description SchemaError

If a value cannot be coerced (e.g. "abc" → int) or a required non-nullable field is missing.

Stops at the first row that fails validation.

required strict bool

items.title: Normalizer
items.text:
Normalizer(**data: Any)

Bases: interloper.serializable.base.Serializable

Type-native normalizer for list[dict] asset data.

Applies optional transformations to rows (column-name normalization, nested-dict flattening, missing-column fill). The shapes an asset may return besides rows (a generator, models, a lone dict) are unwrapped by the asset before normalization, so a normalizer only ever reshapes rows.

Normalizer is Serializable so instances round-trip through Spec with their concrete subclass intact — e.g. across the host → child-pod DAG-spec boundary.

Usage:

@asset(normalizer=Normalizer())
def my_asset(context):
    return [{"UserName": "alice", "Address": {"City": "NYC"}}]

Attributes:

Name Type Description normalize_columns_names

Convert column names to snake_case.

flatten_max_level

Maximum nesting depth to flatten. 0 disables flattening, None flattens without limit, a positive int flattens up to that many levels.

flatten_separator

Separator for flattened key names.

fill_missing

Fill missing keys across rows with None so every row has the same columns.

replace_empty_dicts

Replace {} values with None.

replace_empty_strings

Replace "" values with None.

drop_na_columns

Drop columns where every value is None.

snake_case_digits

Treat digit groups as words when snake-casing column names (acosClicks14d → acos_clicks_14d instead of acos_clicks14d). Off by default because the right convention depends on the upstream API's naming semantics.

column_overrides

Explicit raw-name → normalized-name mapping, applied before the snake_case conversion. For API quirk names no general rule can handle (eCPAddToCart → ecp_add_to_cart).

items.title: Sources
items.text: A source owns a set of assets and the connection, config and destinations they share.

items.title: source
items.text:
source(target: Any = None, /, **settings: Any) -> Any

Create a Source subclass from a decorated class or function.

A decorated class declares its configuration fields, its assets (methods carrying @asset) and its helpers; a decorated function returns the asset classes and turns its own annotated parameters into configuration fields:

@source(tags=["Advertising"], dataset="raw_shop", relations={"connection": ShopConnection})
class Shop(Source): ...

relations maps a relation name to a Relation, a component class (the shorthand for a relation on it), or a list of component classes narrowing the relation Source declares under that name; explicit declarations win over the ones read from the class annotations.

Every other keyword is definition metadata or behaviour: the public ClassVars and field defaults Source declares (key, name, icon, tags, dataset, default_destination_key, normalizer, materialization_strategy, ...). An unknown name is a TypeError at decoration. The result is a Source subclass with its assets discovered.

items.title: Source
items.text:
Source(**data: Any)

Bases: interloper.component.base.Component, interloper.operation.base.Workload

A grouping component that holds assets with shared relations and destinations.

Define a source by subclassing: an annotation naming a component class declares a relation the source's assets inherit, and asset_types (or asset classes written in the body) names what it materializes:

class MySource(Source):
    connection: MyConnection
    asset_types = [Users, Orders]

An asset is reached by its key: on the class it is the asset class, on an instance the live asset (see AssetMeta):

MySource.users      # the asset class
MySource().users    # this source's Asset with key "users"

Assets written in the class body are the typed form; one given only in asset_types is reached the same way at runtime.

items.title: asset_types
items.text:
asset_types = []

Built-in mutable sequence.

If no argument is given, the constructor creates a new empty list. The argument must be an iterable if specified.

items.title: destinations
items.text:
destinations = Relation(
    kind="destination",
    key="",
    many=True,
    optional=True,
    default=None,
    on_delete="block",
    name="destinations",
)

One declared link from an owner component to the components that may fill it.

kind and key name the acceptable targets: kind names one or several component kinds, key (when non-empty) narrows to specific keys within those kinds, matched through ComponentIdentity.satisfies. many marks a relation that binds several components at once; optional marks one that may stay unbound or be left empty, and says nothing else: on_delete alone decides what deleting a bound target does, block refusing the deletion while this relation holds the target and detach letting it through and dropping the binding. default and has_fallback together describe a relation that can be resolved without an explicit binding.

A relation is also its own descriptor: Component._collect installs the stamped copy under the relation's name, so the class attribute reads as the declaration and the instance attribute as what is bound to it, and assignment rebinds it.

The declaration form the framework writes pairs the relation with the annotation of what fills it (destinations: list[Destination] = Relation("destination", many=True)). The TYPE_CHECKING __new__ is what makes that form check: the type checker reads a Pydantic field of the annotated type, so the constructor kwarg and the instance attribute are both typed, while the runtime sees a Relation (Pydantic ignores it, and Component._collect drops the annotation before fields are collected).

Two attributes are not declared but derived. name is stamped from the attribute the relation is declared under, and target is the class the Relation(cls) shorthand was written with, the class a fallback is built from; neither is a constructor argument. default (intended type Callable[[], Component] | None) and target (intended type type[Component] | None) are typed Any for the type checker, since Component is only imported under TYPE_CHECKING; both stay out of dumps.

model_post_init(context: Any) -> None

Build the source's assets, own them, check where they land, and wire them to each other.

The assets are incomplete when built here: this source's own relation kwargs, which they read through it, are bound only after model_post_init returns. That is why nothing is validated at construction; validate_relations cascades into each asset when the DAG or reconstruction asks, with everything this source can fill already bound.

items.title: table
items.text:
table(asset: Asset) -> str

The physical table name of one of this source's assets.

A reference's table is its table_name as written, with this source's fields filled in by format. Any other asset's is the asset key suffixed with the instance's discriminator (the config field marked discriminator=True) and coerced to a valid identifier, so instances of a multi-account source materialize side by side in one dataset instead of overwriting each other's data. Without a discriminator the asset key is used as-is.

Override for another composition; keep the {asset.key}__{suffix} shape so tables stay wildcard-queryable per asset, leave references to super(), and return a valid identifier: the result is validated when the source resolves its assets, not coerced.

required

validate_relations(
    nodes: Mapping[str, Component] | None = None,

An asset this source does not materialize is only ever read, so what fills its own relations is nothing any run needs: it is left unchecked, the same position _check_relations takes on a node it only reads. That is what keeps a source reconstructible from a partial set of assets, where a read-only asset names a sibling the document does not carry.

items.title: run
items.text:
run(coro: Coroutine[Any, Any, _T]) -> _T

Run a coroutine to completion from synchronous code.

The sync bridge to the async-native engine. It backs the sync entrypoints — asset.run(), asset.materialize(), dag.materialize() — and can be called directly to drive any other framework coroutine (e.g. a configured runner) from a script, a REPL, or a notebook cell without touching asyncio:

import interloper as il

result = il.run(il.AsyncRunner(max_workers=8).run(dag))

Unlike asyncio.run, this works where an event loop is already running (Jupyter) and reuses one persistent background loop across calls, so loop-bound clients cached on connections stay valid from one invocation to the next. Async code should await the coroutine directly instead.

Ctrl-C cancels the coroutine before re-raising KeyboardInterrupt.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default coro Coroutine[Any, Any, _T]

The coroutine to execute.

required

Returns:

Type Description _T

The coroutine's result.

Raises:

Type Description RuntimeError

If called from code already running on the bridge's own loop (await instead — blocking would deadlock).

KeyboardInterrupt

Re-raised after cancelling the coroutine.

items.title: bounded_gather
items.text:
bounded_gather(
    coros: Iterable[Coroutine[Any, Any, _T]], *, limit: int
) -> list[_T]

Await coroutines concurrently, capped at limit in flight at once.

Results are returned in the order the coroutines were given (like asyncio.gather), but at most limit run concurrently — the bound is what keeps fan-out (paginated pages, per-entity requests) from stampeding an API into rate limits. If any coroutine raises, the exception propagates and the rest are cancelled.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default coros Iterable[Coroutine[Any, Any, _T]]

The coroutines to run.

required limit int

Maximum number of coroutines in flight at once (must be >= 1).

required

Returns:

Type Description list[_T]

The results, ordered to match coros.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If limit is less than 1.

items.title: import_from_path
items.text:
import_from_path(path: str) -> Any

Import an object from a path.

Two forms are supported:

  • Dotted path — "module.submodule.ClassName": imports the parent module, then does a single getattr for the final name.
  • Composite path — "module.submodule:ClassName.nested": the colon marks the module / attribute boundary explicitly. Everything before : is imported as a module, everything after is a chain of getattr calls on the imported object. This is the form emitted by Asset.classpath for source-owned assets so that the asset class can be reached via a class-level descriptor without instantiating its parent source.

items.title: Web UI
items.text: The platform ships a web application over the components the framework defines: browse what is installed, configure sources and their credentials, attach destinations, schedule jobs, react to outcomes with hooks, and follow every run down to its events. Nothing on these screens is written per connector; each page is rendered from component definitions, as Generated from definitions explains. This page walks through the app with the demo sources that ship with the framework.

items.title: Timeline
items.text: The landing page: one row per job and per source, one bar per run over a selectable window, green for success and red for failure. Hovering a bar shows the run; clicking opens it.

items.title: Graph
items.text: The lineage of every asset in the organisation, built from the dependency relations the framework infers (a feeds b, c, d, which feed e). Nodes carry the asset's tags and its health; the toolbar groups by asset, by source instance or by source type, and filters by status. Selecting a node opens a panel with the asset's schema, partitioning, destinations and last runs.

items.title: Collection
items.text: Every source instance and its assets, grouped by source type. Columns show the last run, the connection, the number of upstream dependencies, the destinations and the jobs that target each asset. The catalog of installed but not yet configured types is reachable from the "New source" button.

items.title: Sources
items.text: The configured source instances. Two instances of the same type ("Demo Data" and "Demo Flaky") coexist because each has its own dataset; with a discriminator field they would also have distinct table names.

items.title: Creating a source
items.text:
The wizard opens on the type step: one tile per source definition in the catalog, grouped by tag, with the icon and name the class declares. Selecting a tile advances.

The assets step lists the definition's assets with their docstrings and tags, filterable by tag. The selection becomes the source's children; assets left out stay available as dependencies.

One step per resource relation the source declares. It lists the existing connections of the required key or creates one inline; the connection form is the same as on the Connections page.

The details step recaps the earlier choices and renders the form generated from the source's configuration fields: the framework's own (materialization_strategy, dataset) and the class's (hello, random_failure_probability on the demo source), with the labels, descriptions and tooltips their field helpers declare.

items.title: Connections
items.text:
Credentials, stored encrypted and shared by every source that needs them. The page lists the configured connections and, below, the catalog of connection types installed. The sidebar entry exists because the catalog contains the connection resource kind; a package defining another kind gets its own entry.

A connection declaring OAuthConfig gets a sign-in tab when the provider's app credentials are configured on the server, and a manual tab showing every field. The auto_renew toggle appears because the class is renewable; a "Test connection" action appears when it implements check().

items.title: Destinations
items.text: Where data lands. A destination's form comes from its configuration fields, and its connection relation, when it declares one, is a picker over the matching connections.

items.title: Jobs
items.text: Cron jobs over sources or assets. The schedule column renders the cron expression and its timezone; "Next run at" and "Last run at" are the job's state model, shown as columns because the definition publishes a state_schema. The job form uses the cron and timezone widgets and the partition-window fields (lookback, offset); its Operation section carries concurrency, how many of a firing's partitions run at once.

items.title: Hooks
items.text: Reactions to run and backfill outcomes: a webhook posting failures to an operations endpoint, and a trigger hook starting the monthly rollup when the daily job completes. The watched components and, for trigger hooks, the targets are relation pickers derived from the hook class's vocabulary.

items.title: Executions
items.text:
Every run with its target, partition key, status and timings. Runs come from schedules, manual triggers, hooks and backfills.

A backfill is one run per partition over a range, dispatched newest first with a concurrency cap; the range is shown in the target's partition-key shape, and the Partitions column draws each partition's latest attempt by status, the same bar the runs table draws for a run's assets. Both tables filter by status, and a status still executing spins.

items.title: Run detail
items.text: One run: the per-asset execution timeline (or the run's graph), and the full event stream the framework emitted, filterable to lifecycle events, errors or the log lines assets wrote through context.logger. A stack's latest attempt, when it failed, offers "Retry failed" and "Retry all".

items.title: Search and switching
items.text: The search box (⌘K) opens a command palette over every page, source, job and hook, with aliases (typing "DAG" finds the graph). The footer switches the organisation and the user, and toggles light and dark mode.

items.title: Connecting MCP clients
items.text: The platform runs an MCP server (interloper-mcp, served at /mcp) that gives an AI client the same view of an organisation the app has: the catalog, the collection, lineage, runs and backfills, and, for editors, the writes. A client authenticates in one of two ways: it signs in through OAuth, or it is handed a personal access token.

items.title: Connecting claude.ai
items.text:
claude.ai and any other MCP client that supports remote servers connect as a custom connector, with nothing to copy between the two sides.

  1. In the client, add a custom connector and enter the MCP endpoint as its URL, for example https://app.example.com/mcp.
  2. The client discovers the authorization server on its own, registers itself with it, and opens the app's consent page in a browser.
  3. Sign in to the app if you are not already, check that the application named on the page is the one you just started, and approve.
  4. The client returns with an access token and a refresh token and keeps itself signed in.

The consent page names the application, where it returns you to and the account it will act as. Approve only a connection you started.

A connection acts as you, in every organisation you belong to, with the role you hold in each: an editor can use the write tools in the organisations where they are editor and only read in the others, and a role change applies to the connection at once. Every tool takes an organisation argument naming the organisation it acts in (an id from list_organisations), which can be left out when you belong to exactly one.

items.title: Revoking a connection
items.text: Open Settings, Authentication, Authorised apps. Each application you have approved is listed; revoking one ends its refresh token and its access tokens straight away, and it must ask for your consent again to reconnect.

items.title: Lifetimes
items.text:
Access tokens are short lived and refresh tokens replace themselves on every use, so a client that stays in use never asks you again. Both lifetimes are settings:

Setting Default Meaning auth.access_token_expiry_minutes 60 Minutes an OAuth access token stays valid. auth.refresh_token_expiry_days 30 Days a refresh token stays valid, counted again from each rotation.

A client idle for longer than the refresh lifetime has to ask for consent again. Presenting a refresh token that was already used is treated as theft: the whole chain it belongs to is revoked.

items.title: Personal access tokens
items.text: A client that cannot run a browser flow (a script, a CI job, an older MCP client) takes a personal access token instead. Create one under Settings, Authentication, Personal Access Tokens, and send it as Authorization: Bearer <token>. The token is shown once, acts as you in every organisation you belong to with your role in each, and works until it expires or you revoke it on the same page. Treat it like a password.

items.title: The deployment
items.text:
Both sides need to know where they are reachable.

  • server.external_url (INTERLOPER_SERVER_EXTERNAL_URL, the chart's externalUrl) is the public base URL of the app. It is the issuer of the authorization server, whose metadata the API serves at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, and the MCP server names it as the authorization server in its own metadata. Every pod of the deployment gets it.
  • The MCP endpoint's public URL is the resource clients sign in to. It is /mcp on the app's public URL, https://app.example.com/mcp, where the chart serves it. Set mcp.external_url (INTERLOPER_MCP_EXTERNAL_URL, the chart's mcp.externalUrl) only when the endpoint lives elsewhere; the API and the MCP server both read it, so the resource the MCP server advertises is the one the authorization server accepts.

The chart's HTTPRoute sends /mcp and /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource to the MCP service and /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server to the API, all on the app hostnames. The Ingress sends the authorization server's metadata to the API as well; it does not route the MCP endpoint, so an Ingress deployment that serves MCP clients adds those routes itself.

Outside the chart, interloper app, the compose stack's nginx and the Nuxt dev server route /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server to the API too, and make dev-up and the compose stack set server.external_url to the address the browser opens.

Without server.external_url, the issuer falls back to http://localhost:<port>, which serves a local development instance and nothing else. The API and the MCP server derive it, and the MCP resource under it, the same way, so the issuer the MCP server names is the one the API serves.

The metadata, registration, token and revocation endpoints answer cross-origin requests from any origin, without credentials, so a client running in a browser (MCP Inspector) can sign in. The authorization and consent steps stay on the app's own origin.

items.title: Signing in to the API
items.text: The authorization server also issues tokens for the HTTP API, for an application that calls it rather than the MCP server (the Slack backend, a connector a vendor hosts). Such a client names the API as the resource of its authorization request, <issuer>/api, for example https://app.example.com/api, and sends the access token it receives as Authorization: Bearer <token> on /api/... calls. A token is bound to the one resource it was granted for: an API token is refused by the MCP server, and an MCP token by the API. Every authorization request names exactly one resource; a trailing slash on it is ignored. Such a client usually has a fixed client id and secret, registered as below.

items.title: Registering a client yourself
items.text:
A client that registers itself needs no setup, and it is shown to the user by the name it gave. An application that cannot, because it is configured with a fixed client id and secret (a Slack app, a connector a vendor hosts), is registered by an operator from the command line:

interloper oauth create --name "Acme connector" \
    --redirect-uri https://connector.example.com/oauth/callback

The command prints the client_id and the client_secret. The secret is shown once and cannot be recovered: only its hash is stored, so a lost secret means deleting the client and creating another. Repeat --redirect-uri to register several. A redirect URI must be https, http on localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1], or the private-use scheme of a known client (cursor, vscode, vscode-insiders, windsurf); the same rule applies to clients that register themselves. A request must name a registered redirect URI exactly, except that a loopback http one matches on any port, since a native app picks a free port for each sign-in.

interloper oauth list
interloper oauth delete <client_id>

list shows the clients an operator registered, not the ones that registered themselves. delete removes a client together with its codes and refresh tokens and revokes its access tokens for every user, so nothing it was given keeps working. The commands read and write the database the settings point at, so run them where the database is configured, like interloper db. Every flag is in CLI.

items.title: Generated from definitions
items.text:
The web UI contains no per-connector code. Every tile, wizard step, form field and status column is derived from the same component definitions the framework builds for the catalog. Add a source or a connection to a package, register it with an entry point, and the UI knows how to list, create, configure, check and run it.

This page follows the data from a component class to the screen.

items.title: From class to catalog
items.text:
Every component class describes itself through definition(): kind, key, import path, display name, icon, tags, the docstring as description, the JSON Schema of its configuration fields, the JSON Schema of its state model, and its relation vocabulary. The API serves the catalog as JSON, to the members of an organisation ({org_id}), whose editors may also run the checks:

Endpoint Returns GET /api/organisations/{org_id}/catalog Every enabled definition, keyed by component key. GET /api/organisations/{org_id}/catalog/resource-kinds The resource kinds present (connection, config, …). POST /api/organisations/{org_id}/catalog/{key}/check A live check of a connection's unsaved config. POST /api/organisations/{org_id}/catalog/{key}/resolve The options of a provider-backed FetchField. GET /api/oauth/providers Which OAuth providers have in-house app credentials configured.

The app loads the catalog once and reads everything below from it. The sidebar's "Entities" section is built from the resource kinds: a package that defines a new resource kind gets its own page without any UI change.

items.title: Tiles
items.text:
Type pickers render one tile per definition, grouped by the first tag when definitions carry tags. The tile shows icon, name and the first line of the docstring, and search matches name, key, description and tags.

@il.source(name="Facebook Ads", icon="logos:facebook", tags=["Advertising"])
class FacebookAds(il.Source):
    """Campaigns, ads and their daily statistics from the Marketing API."""

renders as an "Advertising" tile labelled "Facebook Ads" with the Facebook logo.

items.title: Wizard steps
items.text:
Creating or editing any component runs through one definition-driven stepper. The steps come from the definition:

Step Derived from Type The kind's definitions, when several classes exist and none is pinned. Assets (sources only) SourceDefinition.assets: one row per asset with its schema and partitioning; the selection becomes the source's children. An asset relation reaching another source is resolved against existing sources. One step per orchestration relation relations entries the page asks for, such as a job's targets or a hook's watches, restricted to the kind the relation allows. One step per resource relation Each relation whose kind is connection, config or resource: the step lists existing instances of its key and offers to create one inline. Destination (sources only) The key list of the destinations relation: the destination classes the source allows. Details Name plus the form generated from config_schema.

Relation semantics are enforced the same way when the platform stores an edge: kind, key, many, optional and the on_delete policy described in the component model.

items.title: Forms
items.text:
The details step, the inline resource creation and the edit drawer all render SchemaForm, a generic form over config_schema. Widgets resolve from the field helpers' extensions first and from the JSON Schema type otherwise:

Field helper Extension Widget InputField x-widget: text Text input. SecretField x-widget: password Masked input with a reveal toggle. TextField x-widget: textarea Multi-line textarea. JsonField x-widget: json Monospace editor; the value is parsed as JSON when it is valid. CronField x-widget: cron Expression input with presets and a human-readable rendering in the sibling timezone. TimezoneField x-widget: timezone Searchable IANA picker, defaulting to the user's profile timezone. SelectField(options=...) x-widget: select, x-options Dropdown of fixed options. SelectField(options_from="destinations") x-options-from Dropdown fed by the components configured in the same wizard; hidden when there are none. FetchField(provider=...) x-widget: fetch, x-fetch Dropdown whose options are fetched from the service (below). plain bool field Switch. plain int or float field Number input honouring ge and le. plain list[str] field Tag input, or multi-select when items are an enum. Enum-typed field Dropdown of the enum values. nested model field (e.g. retry: RetryPolicy \| None) The model's own fields in a bordered group; an optional model sits behind a switch (off saves null, on starts from the model's defaults).

Presentation keywords carry over: label is the form label, description the help line under it, info a tooltip next to the label. required follows the pydantic definition, and the form is only submittable when every required field has a value.

items.title: Order and sections
items.text:
Fields render in the schema's property order, which lists a component's own fields before those it inherits (see Fields). Fields carrying x-section render under that section's separator, after the fields without one; sections appear in the order their first field does. Sources group dataset and the default destination under "Destination", and their materialization strategy under "Materialization"; a cron job's window fields sit under "Partitioning"; enabled and retry, which the operation, job and source bases declare, sit under "Operation", joined there by a job's cron expression and timezone. A connection's only operation is its renewal, so it hides enabled (Automatic renewal is the switch) and keeps retry beside Automatic renewal among its credentials; a connection with nothing to renew shows neither. A connection's sign-in tabs, the OAuth sign-in and the credential fields they govern render together in one bordered group.

A page can replace a section's generated fields through the wizard's #section-<name> slot (the section name lowercased, e.g. #section-partitioning). The slot receives the section's field keys and the schema, plus the wizard's extra contract: extra.config merges into the saved config and extra.valid gates submit. The job wizard uses it to show the partition window only when the selected targets are partitioned, with a preview of what a run covers.

items.title: Fetched options
items.text: A FetchField(provider="connection.accounts") renders as a dropdown that fills itself once the connection relation is filled. The form posts the component key, the field name and that component's credentials to POST /api/organisations/{org_id}/catalog/{key}/resolve; the API reads the provider reference from its own copy of the schema (never from the client), instantiates the resource, calls the method, and returns the items. Only methods marked @fetch_field_provider may be called this way. Until the relation is filled, the field degrades to a text input.

items.title: OAuth sign-in
items.text: A connection with an OAuthConfig carries an x-oauth extension at the root of its schema. When the provider's in-house credentials are configured on the server, the form shows two tabs: "Sign in with X", which hides the mapped credential fields and shows a sign-in button, and "Manual", which shows every field. After sign-in the returned token lands in the field mapped to the refresh_token role; the client id and secret are resolved on the server and never reach the browser.

items.title: Instance names
items.text:
The field marked discriminator=True (x-discriminator) names the instance: the wizard proposes the selected option's label (an ad account name rather than its id) as the component name, and the platform derives the per-instance table names from the same value.

The value itself stays visible: every component response carries it as discriminator, the sources table shows it under the name and matches it in the search box, the command palette lists it next to the type, and a fetched option shows its id under its label in the picker. A user holding an account id from the warehouse or the vendor finds the source by it.

items.title: State columns
items.text: A kind with a state_model publishes state_schema. List pages add one column per property: jobs show next_run_at and last_run_at, connections show next_renewal_at, last_renewed_at and last_renewal_error, hooks show last_fired_at and last_error. Properties flagged x-hidden are plumbing and stay out of the table.

items.title: Actions the definition advertises
items.text: Definition field UI ResourceDefinition.checkable A "Test connection" action calling POST /api/organisations/{org_id}/catalog/{key}/check, which runs the class's check() against the unsaved form values and surfaces ConnectionCheckError messages under the fields. ResourceDefinition.renewable A "Renew now" action and the auto_renew toggle; both disappear for classes without a renewal flow. AssetDefinition.partitioning Partition pickers on manual runs and backfills, with the granularity's key shape (2026-08, 2026-08-21, …). AssetDefinition.asset_schema The column list shown for each asset.

items.title: Drift
items.text: Persisted components reference catalog keys. When a key no longer resolves, because the class was renamed or removed (missing) or is not enabled in this deployment's catalog (disabled), the component is shown with a drift status instead of failing to load, and the Sources page offers a confirmed cleanup. See interloper_db.ComponentDriftError in Errors.

items.title: What a package author gets
items.text:
Writing this, and nothing else:

@il.connection(name="Shop API", icon="carbon:shopping-cart", tags=["Commerce"])
class ShopConnection(il.Connection):
    api_key: str = il.SecretField(description="API key from the shop admin")

    @il.fetch_field_provider
    async def stores(self) -> list[dict]: ...

    async def check(self) -> bool: ...


@il.source(name="Shop", icon="carbon:shopping-cart", tags=["Commerce"])
class Shop(il.Source):
    """Orders and customers from the shop API."""

    connection: ShopConnection

    store_id: str = il.FetchField(provider="connection.stores", label_key="name", value_key="id", discriminator=True)
    ...

gives the UI: a "Commerce" tile for the source and the connection; a connection form with a masked key and a working "Test connection" button; a source wizard whose connection step lists existing Shop API connections or creates one inline, whose asset step lists the source's assets with their schemas, and whose details step shows a store dropdown filled from the API; an instance named after the chosen store; and a table per store in the destination. Every later change to the class flows through on the next deploy.

items.title: Running the app
items.text: The web UI is part of the platform: a FastAPI backend, a Postgres database, a scheduler, and the Nuxt single-page app served as static assets. The core framework does not need any of it; the platform needs the core.

items.title: Packages
items.text: Package Role interloper-db Persistence and migrations. interloper-api The HTTP backend the UI talks to. interloper-scheduler Cron controller, hook evaluator, credential renewal, queue worker, reaper, launchers. interloper-app The built SPA, served by the API process.

items.title: Images
items.text:
Every release publishes one image per role to ghcr.io/digitl-cloud, plus a Helm chart that deploys them. Each image comes in two variants:

Tag Carries interloper-<role>:<version> Loaded: the role's own packages, every component class a catalog can name (ready-made sources, BigQuery and GCS destinations, the Slack hook) and what the role runs on (both launchers on the scheduler, the agent on the api, telemetry). interloper-<role>:<version>-slim Slim: interloper-core plus the role's own packages, nothing optional. No sources, no destinations, no launcher beyond in-process, no telemetry SDK.

The roles are api, scheduler, core, mcp and frontend (nginx, single variant). The loaded images are what the Helm chart deploys and what a deployment configured from the catalog wants: launcher.type and agent.enabled select between things already in the image, so switching one is a restart and never a rebuild.

core is the framework itself, with no platform around it: the Kubernetes runner uses it as the per-asset Job target, and interloper-core:<version>-slim is interloper-core and nothing else, which makes it the base to build on when you ship your own components.

Two rules decide what a loaded image carries. Any role that builds a catalog must be able to import every class the catalog can name, which is why the api and mcp ship sources, destinations and hooks they never execute: they describe them, and a class that fails to import is skipped with a warning rather than an error, so the answer would quietly be wrong. The vendor SDKs (bingads, facebook-business, google-ads) are the exception, because the asset modules guard those imports: only the roles that actually execute assets, scheduler and core, carry them. That single distinction is why the api and mcp images are a fraction of the size of the two that run assets.

items.title: Extending an image
items.text:
The slim images exist to be built on. Every package is on PyPI, so adding what a deployment needs is an install in a child image:

FROM ghcr.io/digitl-cloud/interloper-scheduler:<version>-slim

USER root
RUN pip --python /interloper/.venv/bin/python install --no-cache-dir \
      "interloper-assets[google]" \
      interloper-google-cloud \
      my-own-connectors
USER app

The --python flag matters, and it goes before the subcommand. The application lives in the virtualenv at /interloper/.venv, which was built by uv and therefore has no pip of its own; a bare pip install would resolve to the base image's interpreter instead and land the package somewhere the app never looks, with no error to show for it.

Anything installed this way registers itself: a package declaring components under the interloper.components entry point joins the catalog on the next start, with no change to the image's command. List what you want enabled under catalog and the deployment sees exactly that, as described in Catalog and Entry points & registries.

The same recipe works on a loaded image when you want everything it ships plus your own components.

items.title: One process per role
items.text:
Each role starts through the command its package contributes, which is what the images run:

interloper api --no-create-tables                                  # the api image: the HTTP API
interloper scheduler --cron --worker --reaper --no-create-tables   # the scheduler image: cron (with hooks and renewal), worker, reaper

interloper scheduler takes --no-cron, --no-worker and --no-reaper to split its services across replicas: cron and the reaper are singletons, the worker scales out, and replicas split the work through row locks. Without a flag, a service follows its enabled setting (cron.enabled, worker.enabled, reaper.enabled), which every pod reading the same interloper.yaml shares; that is why the images and the chart name all three.

items.title: One process
items.text:
interloper app --api --cron --worker --reaper

runs every service in one process against the configured Postgres, serving the UI on port 3000. It needs interloper-app installed. Each service can be toggled off on its own, and --dev runs the Nuxt dev server with hot reload instead of the built assets.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
interloper.yaml in the working directory, or INTERLOPER_* variables:

postgres:
  host: localhost
  user: interloper
  database: interloper          # password: INTERLOPER_POSTGRES_PASSWORD

auth:
  google_client_id: ...
  google_client_secret: ...
  google_redirect_uri: https://app.example.com/api/auth/google/callback
  allowed_domains: [example.com]

catalog:
  - my_package.sources.Shop
  - interloper_assets.facebook_ads.connector.source.FacebookAds

The file is not interpolated: a field left out of a block is read from its INTERLOPER_<SECTION>_<FIELD> variable, which is where secrets go. INTERLOPER_ENCRYPTION_KEY is required: resource configs are encrypted at rest, and the Google login signs the cookie it keeps between Google's two legs with a key derived from it, so every replica can finish a login another one started. Login is Google OAuth. allowed_domains restricts who may sign up; super_admin_emails bootstraps platform administrators, promoted by interloper db init and at login (promote-only). Once one exists, super-admins grant and revoke the access from the admin portal's Users page. In-house OAuth app credentials for connectors live in INTERLOPER_<PROVIDER>_CLIENT_ID and _CLIENT_SECRET; a provider without them has no sign-in tab, only manual credential entry. Its redirect URI, to register in the provider console, is <server.external_url>/auth/<provider>, unless INTERLOPER_<PROVIDER>_REDIRECT_URI overrides it. The full settings list is in Settings. With the Helm chart, each key of the release Secret (secrets) reaches every interloper pod as the variable of the same name; the root-level extraEnv maps keys from other Secrets one by one.

items.title: Database
items.text:
interloper db init          # create the database, tables and run migrations; idempotent
interloper db upgrade       # migrate an existing database to head

The serving commands (interloper api, interloper scheduler, interloper app) also create missing tables on startup unless --no-create-tables is passed.

items.title: Local development
items.text: The repository ships a dev harness: make dev provisions a local Postgres database, seeds a super-admin, an organisation, the demo source and a daily job, and starts every service with the Nuxt dev server on port 3000. make compose-up does the same in Docker. The screenshots on the Tour come from that harness with a few more demo components added.
